subtype: Approach: putting it off until the last moment [Pitfall]
passage: I kept waiting for the right moment to tell my parents about the job in Toronto, and the right moment never came. On every Sunday call I opened my mouth and asked about the neighbours instead. Then, three weeks before my visa interview, my aunt phoned Amma. "Ganga is going abroad, didn't she tell you?" Amma called me that night and her voice was quiet. "Why did I hear it from Bua?" I tried to say I had been protecting them. It sounded thin. It was not the moving that hurt; it was the finding out. It took Papa two days to speak to me. I think if I had told them in March, they would have cried and then helped me pack. Instead I had to earn back something I had not known I could lose. - Ganga

qa.q: Who told Amma about the job abroad?
qa.a: Ganga's aunt, Bua, phoned Amma and told her.

qa.q: What was Amma feeling when she asked "Why did I hear it from Bua?"
qa.a: Amma felt hurt and shut out, and her voice was quiet.

qa.q: What could Ganga do now to repair things?
qa.a: Ganga could apologise sincerely for not telling them, share the plans and a visiting schedule, and listen to their worries.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt during the two days before he spoke?
qa.a: Papa may have felt hurt and disappointed, taking time to gather himself before talking.

grounding: Ganga delays telling the parents about moving abroad until a relative does, and the way they learn hurts trust more than the decision.

subtype: Approach: putting it off until the last moment [Pitfall]
passage:
Counsellor's note, study-abroad office, 12 May.
Jyoti came in today, not about her visa, which is approved, but about her parents. She had planned to tell them about the Toronto admission "after everything was final". She kept waiting: after the offer, after the loan, after the visa. Last Sunday a cousin congratulated her mother at a wedding, in front of the whole family. Her mother came home and didn't speak to her for two days.
Jyoti said, "They're not angry that I'm going. They're angry that my aunt knew before them." She cried for most of the session.
We talked about how the delay, more than the decision, is what hurt. She has decided to sit with her parents tonight, apologise for the delay without defending it, and ask what they would like to know. I have booked her in again for Friday.
— Neelam

qa.q: When had Jyoti planned to tell her parents?
What was Jyoti feeling in the session?
qa.a: Jyoti was upset and remorseful, crying for most of the session because her parents were hurt at hearing it from others.

qa.q: What would have worked better than waiting until everything was final?
qa.a: Telling her parents early, perhaps once the admission came, so they heard it from her and could be part of the process.

qa.q: How did Jyoti's mother likely feel at the wedding?
qa.a: She was likely embarrassed and hurt to learn such big news from a relative in public, which is why she stayed silent for two days.

grounding: It shows a young woman delaying telling her parents about moving abroad until they hear it from a relative, so trust is hurt more than by the decision.

subtype: Approach: putting it off until the last moment [Pitfall]
passage:
Trisha's diary, 3 September, late.
Mummy called at 7 pm. Not to ask. To tell me she had just heard from Naveen, my cousin, that I'm moving to Berlin in November. Naveen saw my "new role" post on the job site and phoned his mother, who phoned mine.
I had a plan. Tell them at Dussehra, face to face, once the contract was signed and the flat sorted. I kept pushing it back because every time I pictured Papa's face I felt sick. Now Papa won't come to the phone.
Mummy said, "Berlin we could have got used to. But Naveen knew first, Trisha. Naveen." That line keeps playing in my head.
I made it so much worse by waiting. Tomorrow I'm taking the early train home to say sorry properly.

qa.q: How did Naveen find out about the move?
qa.a: Naveen saw the "new role" post on the job site.

qa.q: Why did Trisha keep pushing the talk back?
qa.a: Every time Trisha pictured Papa's face, the dread felt sickening, so waiting seemed easier.

qa.q: What is Trisha's best step now?
qa.a: Going home in person to apologise for the delay, then listening to how Mummy and Papa feel before explaining the move.

qa.q: What hurt Mummy more than the move itself?
qa.a: Mummy was hurt that Naveen knew first; the move could be accepted, but hearing it second-hand felt like being shut out.

grounding: It shows someone delaying telling their parents about moving abroad until a relative tells them first, so the news lands worse and trust is hurt.
